title: Valuation Rings and Discrete Valuation Rings

items.title: Totally ordered abelian groups
Valuations on a field
Valuation rings
A valuation ring is local
items.strategy: The nonunits are exactly the elements whose inverses stay outside the ring. Valuation comparability makes that set an ideal, and every element outside it is automatically a unit.

items.title: Characterizations of valuation rings
items.strategy: Compare the fraction condition, divisibility comparability, and linear ordering of ideals elementwise. Once two generators are always comparable by divisibility, one of them generates the ideal they span, and induction handles finite generation.

items.title: The value group of a valuation ring
A valuation ring is recovered from its value group
items.strategy: Quotient the fraction-field units by the unit group, order cosets by divisibility, and check that the order is representative-independent, total, and translation-invariant. The quotient map is then a valuation whose nonnegative locus is exactly the original ring.

items.title: Valuation rings are integrally closed
items.strategy: If an integral element x lay outside the valuation ring, then x^(-1) would lie in its maximal ideal. Multiplying a monic equation for x by a suitable power of x^(-1) would force 1 into that maximal ideal, a contradiction.

items.title: Discrete valuations
Discrete valuation rings
Uniformising parameters
Every nonzero fraction is a unit times a power of a uniformiser
items.strategy: Choose a uniformiser pi of value 1. For any nonzero element, subtract its value from the corresponding power of pi to produce a unit, and use the valuation to prove the exponent and unit class are unique.

items.title: Ideals in a DVR are powers of the maximal ideal
items.strategy: A nonzero ideal contains an element of least value. The normal form theorem shows that this element is a unit times a power of the uniformiser and divides every other element of the ideal, so it generates the ideal uniquely.

items.title: Prime ideals and dimension of a DVR
items.strategy: Every nonzero prime ideal contains the uniformiser, hence contains the maximal ideal. The ideal classification leaves only (0) and the maximal ideal, so the unique nonzero prime has height one.

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of a DVR
items.strategy: Use the valuation description to obtain the local PID, integrally closed, and one-dimensional properties. For the converse, prove that a one-dimensional Noetherian local normal domain has principal maximal ideal by the usual colon-ideal and determinant-trick argument, then invoke the principal-maximal-ideal criterion.

items.title: A Noetherian valuation ring is a field or a DVR
items.strategy: If the ring is not a field, finite generation of the maximal ideal and divisibility comparability force one generator to divide all the others, so the maximal ideal is principal. The DVR characterization then applies.

items.title: Length and valuation in a DVR
items.strategy: Filter R/(pi^n) by the images of the powers of the maximal ideal. Each successive quotient is one-dimensional over the residue field, so the filtration has length n, and the normal form theorem reduces R/(x) to the case x = u pi^n.

items.title: Height-one localizations of normal Noetherian domains are DVRs
items.strategy: Localize at a height-one prime. Prime-spectrum correspondence makes the localization a one-dimensional local domain, and the localization preserves Noetherianity and integral closedness. The DVR characterization then finishes.

items.title: Every DVR is a PID
items.strategy: Apply the ideal classification to show that every ideal is generated by a power of the uniformiser or is zero.

title: Valuation Rings and Discrete Valuation Rings — Examples

items.title: The p-adic valuation ring
items.strategy: Write each nonzero rational number as p^n times a quotient prime to p, read off the valuation, and identify units and ideals from the unit-times-power normal form.

items.title: Localizing a PID at a nonzero prime
items.strategy: Show that the localization is a local PID whose maximal ideal is the extension of the chosen prime. The DVR characterization then applies directly.

items.title: A cusp local ring is not a DVR
items.strategy: Work in the local ring of k[t^2,t^3] at its cusp maximal ideal, show that t is integral over the ring but not contained in it, and then invoke the normal local DVR criterion to conclude failure.

items.title: A rank-two valuation ring that is not a DVR
items.strategy: Use a valuation with value group Z x Z in lexicographic order. Because the positive cone has no least element, the associated valuation ring cannot be discrete and hence is not a DVR.

items.title: A nondiscrete rank-one valuation from incommensurate values
items.strategy: Take the ordered subgroup of R generated by 1 and sqrt(2), build the corresponding valuation, and observe that the positive cone has no least element even though the order is archimedean.

items.title: Computing the length of R/(pi^n)
items.strategy: Use the standard filtration by powers of the maximal ideal and identify each subquotient with the residue field to compute the exact length.

items.title: Uniformisers and ideal arithmetic in a DVR
items.strategy: Compare two generators of the maximal ideal using the unit-times-power form, then compute sums and intersections of powers from the ideal classification.

items.title: Ideals in a valuation ring are linearly ordered
items.strategy: Compare two principal ideals by their values and then inspect a nondiscrete valuation ring where the positive-value cut defines a genuinely nonprincipal ideal.
